prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect, establishing topological insulators

statement.case_for: I opened with B004 but, having read the ballots, I now prefer the B045 framing with a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio. The core of the discovery is a clean theory-to-experiment arc: the Z2 classification and the prediction of the quantum spin Hall state in graphene by Kane and Mele, followed by the first transport observation of helical edge channels in HgTe by Molenkamp's group. The idea reorganised condensed matter around band topology, has been reproduced over fifteen years in many materials and laboratories, and has spread into photonics, phononics, spintronics and proposals for topological quantum devices. The interpretation is stable, so recognition is mature and arguably overdue, and the 2016 prize on topological phases of matter covered related but distinct work (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz). Mele belongs with Kane because the Z2 theory is their joint work, and leaving him out of a prize that credits Kane's theory is hard to defend.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the credit tree is incomplete whatever we choose. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal that guided Molenkamp's experiment is outside the credited names, 3D topological insulators (Fu-Kane-Mele, Hasan) and the quantum anomalous Hall effect (Xue) are real further steps that a three-person quantum spin Hall prize leaves out, and the Nobel limit of three forces a narrow citation. The 2016 prize also makes some colleagues ask whether topology has already been recognised. If the committee judges the allocation too contested, the optical lattice clock prize (B022) is the cleaner two-person alternative with very broad opening support, and I would not stand in its way.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators first with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as a compact and defensible three-person configuration, while noting the omitted HgTe theorists.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and have moved to it from my own Kane-Molenkamp pairing. My opening left out Mele, and Eriksson's point that Kane and Mele supplied the decisive Z2 theory is persuasive. I share the concern about the omitted Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. I would answer it in the citation, by tying it to the prediction and first observation of the quantum spin Hall effect, rather than by stretching the credit beyond the supplied names.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B045 first with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, so that theory, the 2D experiment and the 3D ARPES discovery are all covered.
responses.response: I see the logic of covering 2D and 3D, but I disagree with adding Hasan at Mele's expense. Hasan's ARPES work is a distinct and later strand, and 3D topological insulators carry their own theory credit (Fu, Kane, Mele) that the trio would leave dangling. Dropping Mele to make room for it makes the prize less coherent than a quantum spin Hall citation, where Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are the natural names.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first and placed B004 third, calling the compound Kane-Molenkamp-Xue set difficult because it mixes different parts of the discovery.
responses.response: I accept Kroll's criticism of B004. The quantum anomalous Hall effect is a separate achievement from the spin Hall effect, and my own opening noted that. I therefore no longer defend the Xue third name, and that is part of why I moved to B045. On clocks, I agree the case is strong and distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes. I still rank it behind topology, because the clock result is an exceptional metrological advance while topological band theory changed how a whole field classifies matter, but I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Pearce placed lattice clocks first and B045 third, with the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio as the most coherent three-person configuration from the supplied names, and flagged the closeness to the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and take the 2016 overlap seriously, but the overlap is in the shared theme of topology, not in the discovery. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz concerned topological phase transitions and the quantised Hall conductance, while the Z2 classification and time-reversal-invariant helical edge states are a different physical mechanism, observed in a different class of systems. Where I differ from Pearce is on ranking: I think this is a stronger case than baryon acoustic oscillations, which have a more diffuse theoretical credit story.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to recognise only the quantum spin Hall effect, or add 3D topological insulators and the quantum anomalous Hall effect, and how that would fit the three-person limit.
How to handle the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction, which lies outside the credited names.
I rely on my own background knowledge of the priority history and have not verified it independently.
Whether the 2016 topology prize reduces the committee's appetite for a further topology prize.
statement.conflict_note: I work in superconducting circuits and direct WACQT at Chalmers, which hosted several researchers linked to the 2025 prize, and I have a documented collaborative link to Chalmers colleagues such as Per Delsing. That bears on B039 (circuit QED), which I ranked second, and I would recuse myself from deciding it. It does not bear on the topological insulator candidates, where no specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile.
